We want to support the mathematics community in turning progress in AI into deeper human understanding and new discoveries. To support that goal, we are contributing $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI, including the results we recently published.

The funding, managed and awarded by the @SimonsFdn will support workshops, conferences, and special programs. We will also provide access to our models and computing resources to Simons Foundation-supported researchers.

items.title: Blue Rose Research's @davidshor reveals how belief that AI could threaten humanity's survival surged...
items.content:
Blue Rose Research's @davidshor reveals how belief that AI could threaten humanity's survival surged from the 30s to 64% in just 6 months, creating an entirely new political issue:

"'Do you believe that AI could eventually become so powerful that it poses a serious threat to humanity’s survival?'"

"We polled this 6 months ago, and it was in the 30s. Today 64% of voters believe that. I’ve been listening to weird EAs tell me this for 10 years. It is now broken to the public consciousness."

"What we’re witnessing is the birth of a brand-new political issue, which I’ve only ever seen once in my career before, with COVID."

"When we do focus groups, the public still doesn’t have very well-formed thoughts about this. They’re picking up information 30 seconds at a time. We’re watching them process it in real time. This is the least important that AI is going to be."

items.title: Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now the leading US open weight model, scoring 26 on the Artificial...
items.content:
Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now the leading US open weight model, scoring 26 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL achieves twice the intelligence of its predecessor, Nemotron 3 Super (13), and does so using ~60% fewer output tokens per task

It launches alongside Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, the first model in its new Bolt family, which scores 21 on the Intelligence Index

Congratulations to @NVIDIAAI on the releases!

Key Takeaways:

➤ Leading US open weight model: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores 26.5, edging out Thinking Machines' Inkling Small (25.7) and ahead of NVIDIA's Nemotron 3 Ultra (23) and Meta's Muse Glimmer (17)

➤ Bolt comes within 2 points of Ultra: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB scores 21, 1.5 points behind Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B A55B (23). The 2 bit memory has about a seventh of Ultra's parameters (74B vs 550B) and a sixth of its active parameters (9B vs 55B)

➤ Super 3.5 VL near lossless in NVFP4: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL releases in NVFP4, scoring within 0.1 points of its BF16 weights on the Intelligence Index, with no component moving by more than 2.6 points

Nemotron 3.5 Super VL details

Context window: 1M tokens
Modalities: Vision and text input; text output
Parameters: 120B / 12B

Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB details

Context window: 256k tokens
Modalities: Vision and text input; text output
Parameters: 74B / 9B

items.title:
The AI Scientist v3 is out: The Agentic Scientist.

GitHub: https://t.co/v2AkZi4Bmt
Blog: https://t....
items.content:
The AI Scientist v3 is out: The Agentic Scientist.

GitHub: https://t.co/v2AkZi4Bmt
Blog: https://t.co/v3Td5yfvBE
arXiv: https://t.co/RuVnAHjMlK

The Agentic Scientist is the 3rd iteration of our automated AI Scientist research system, and the shift this time is from “one agent writes a paper” to “a scaffold of parallel agents orchestrates the full research loop.”

The system now orchestrates a pool of parallel workers that share memory and distilled conclusions. Crucially, it features Evidence Generation: isolated agents automatically run controlled baselines and ablations to prove why an idea actually works.

It works as a co-scientist. We used a development version as a co-scientist to explore biologically plausible learning rules. The agent handled the empirical heavy lifting, proposing mechanisms and running experiments. We stayed in the loop to steer direction, verify results, and moderate claims. That feels like the right division of labor for where the technology actually is.

This resulted in a new biologically plausible learning algorithm, and the resulting paper was accepted at ALIFE 2026 as an oral presentation.

We are also releasing AutoIllustrate. It generates editable https://t.co/i6fwB6vzQV vector figures instead of uneditable, hallucinated raster images. Real scientists need vectors, not pixels. I am an SVG junkie ;)

Incredible work by Robert Lange, Luca Grillotti, Yutaro Yamada, Rujikorn Charakorn, and the team!

Working out how best to use AI in mathematics research—and in science more generally—will take time, effort, and resources. We’re eager to support mathematicians as they drive scientific progress and define the future of their field.

We’ve committed $5 million of funding, compute, and Claude access to help the math community navigate the massive changes that AI brings. We’re partnering with @SimonsFdn, who will manage the award through a community-driven approach, supporting workshops, conferences, and lectures by domain experts.

items.title:
Introducing ExtractBenchPro: the most challenging benchmark for real-world document extraction.

We ...
items.content:
Introducing ExtractBenchPro: the most challenging benchmark for real-world document extraction.

We see a massive long tail of document complexity in terms of use cases brought on from our customers, that are completely unsolved from a price-performance standpoint. These include trial balances, well logs, canvass binders, site plan reviews, duty reconciliations, loss runs, and more.

Most existing extraction benchmarks are saturated by the frontier models (our cheapest modes now score 93%+ on ExtractBench). So there is enormous economic value in building a complex extraction benchmark that reflects this long-tail of knowledge work.

We spent a long time curating the most complex elements that we saw from real world extraction use cases:
✅ Document conventions: containing legends or rules where the rest of the document should be interpreted
✅ Density of internal jargon: specific definitions that must be cross-referenced within a doc
✅ Aggregation and reasoning: beyond returning exact values on a page, infer values derived from aggregating multiple sources of information
✅ Drawn relations: complex diagrams like procedures and circuits
✅ Charts inside documents: read precise points within a chart
✅ Long chart sheets: some data series like well logs cram all this data into an extremely long page

Within the industries where document extraction is relevant, even small mistakes can have enormous negative impacts. Therefore our headline evaluation metric is based on perfect documents: the proportion of docs with perfect (100%) value f1 score.
(Besides this we also measure value f1 and grounded f1)

It’s an extremely hard task for even the latest frontier models to solve, topping out at ~58% or so in Value F1 score for Codex with Astra - which is quite good but extremely expensive (almost $1 per page!) Our LlamaParse agentic/agentic plus modes are 20-40% and cover the left side of the Pareto frontier, at price ranges that are feasible for full production use.

ExtractBenchPro is available today as a website/technical blog, and also on Github and HuggingFace. Check it out!

Website: https://t.co/uRrFNU1Fqo
Hugging Face: https://t.co/1VImPRTorq

items.content:
.@davidshor reveals how AI went from America's least important political issue to being ranked alongside crime, with half its rise since 2024 happening in just 2 days:

"When we first started asking about AI, basically nobody cared. It was ranked 40th out of 40. It was tied with marijuana legalization."

"Then there was this giant spike right around the Coxon event. I was just really used to AI being this weird thing that only nerds care about. The Coxon resignation was a massive event. Billions of social media impressions."

"At this point, AI is ranked 21st out of 40. It’s not top 5. It’s not top 10. But it’s tied with crime. This is a real thing that’s in people’s minds, and it’s something that folks are scared of."

"Basically half of the increase since 2024 happened over a two-day period from the media firestorm around Coxon."

items.title: NVIDIA's RTX Spark N1X puts up to 128 GB of unified memory and a Blackwell GPU in a Windows laptop. ...
items.content:
NVIDIA's RTX Spark N1X puts up to 128 GB of unified memory and a Blackwell GPU in a Windows laptop. In our first AA-AgentPerf-Local results, an RTX Spark laptop completes our local agent workload on Qwen3.8 27B in 18.7 minutes

RTX Spark's N1X chip is essentially the GB10 from DGX Spark (20-core Arm CPU, 6,144-core Blackwell GPU), with up to 128 GB of memory at 300 GB/s. We tested a prototype 15-inch Surface Laptop Ultra (128 GB, $5,900), plugged in with Windows set to high-performance mode, using NVIDIA's published llama.cpp recipes where available

Key results:

➤ On Qwen3.8 27B the RTX Spark laptop finishes our default workload (8 recorded agent tasks, 168 model turns) in 18.7 minutes, close to DGX Spark (17.3), 2.0x faster than the MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 64 GB, 37.6) and 1.8x faster than the AMD Ryzen AI Halo (34.5). The GeForce RTX 5090 desktop is fastest, at 4.9 minutes

➤ On Qwen3.6 35B A3B it takes 7.6 minutes, close to DGX Spark (7.3), and 1.6x faster than the MacBook Pro (11.9)

➤ On Ling 3.0 Flash, the largest current model we test, it takes 15.3 minutes, close to DGX Spark (14.9) and 1.6x faster than the Ryzen AI Halo (25.1). Its 77 GB of weights do not fit on the MacBook Pro or the RTX 5090

Read the full analysis: https://t.co/72xrYNrtw8

items.title: Perplexity's @zbraniecki explains why they're now asking frontier AI models to escape their sandbox ...
items.content:
Perplexity's @zbraniecki explains why they're now asking frontier AI models to escape their sandbox every single day, after discovering an unexpected security vulnerability:

"We asked them to escape, and they couldn’t escape the sandbox, but they were able to bypass a network gateway. They found a way to access a domain they were not supposed to access."

"We secured it. We asked them to try again. They failed. We tried newer models. They failed."

"Then we just started doing this on a daily basis. As our code base evolves, we keep asking agents to try to escape, and that’s one of the mechanisms we use for increased security. It sounds like science fiction, but that’s our reality today."
@perplexity_ai

items.content:
Day-0 LoRA RL is supported on Muse Spark Open: vLLM for rollout, verl FSDP2 for training.

vLLM serves the NVFP4 base with LoRA; the trainer uses a BF16 dequantization of the same weights. R3 replays rollout routing, and only the adapter is updated and synced back.

With GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K, 150 steps on 16 GB300 GPUs improved AIME-2024 mean@8 from 0.56 to 0.85. Train–rollout k3 KL stayed near 2 × 10⁻⁴.

Titan RL also uses vLLM as its rollout engine to provide day-0 RL support.

5/6

items.title: Perplexity's @zbraniecki reveals what happened when they asked Mythos and other frontier AI models t...
items.content:
Perplexity's @zbraniecki reveals what happened when they asked Mythos and other frontier AI models to escape the sandbox designed to contain them:

"It was the moment of feeling like we live in the future, where we were able to just ask the agents to try to escape. And they’ve all tried."

"We could ask them without giving them the source code, without telling them that they're in the sandbox. We could ask them telling them that they’re in the sandbox. We could show them the code and be like, 'Here's what is running you. What do you wanna do with it to get out and get your reward?'"

"We ran it the first time with Mythos, but we ran it with basically all the frontier models. Each one of them approached the problem differently. They were all trying to either exploit known vulnerabilities, or go the easy route first and then try harder and harder."

"It was fun to watch a computer program trying to find a vulnerability in your own code."
@perplexity_ai

items.summary: Anima Anandkumar announces a PNAS paper introducing a recurrent neural operator (RNO) that predicts climate and physical tipping points more than two years in advance with about 11 days of timing error in simulation, also validated on airflow over a tilting wing, with implications for climate modeling and aerospace design.
items.reasoning: Peer-reviewed original research from a top ML researcher (Caltech), with concrete quantitative results and links to the paper and coverage; engagement is modest for the technical nature of the content.
items.summary_html: Anima Anandkumar announces a PNAS paper introducing a recurrent neural operator (RNO) that predicts climate and physical tipping points more than two years in advance with about 11 days of timing error in simulation, also validated on airflow over a tilting wing, with implications for climate modeling and aerospace design.
items.content_html:
The importance of tipping points has been extensively studied, including in a recent @UN @ScienceBoard_UN brief for climate modeling.

But it is challenging to detect tipping points before they happen since they can appear suddenly. We address this in our latest paper appearing in @PNASNews

Our recurrent neural operator tracks the history of changes and can predict the probability of tipping points happening in future and when it is likely to occur.

The RNO was able to look more than two years ahead of the expected tipping point in the simulated data and predict its timing with an error of about 11 days.

The RNO was also run on simulations of airflow over a tilting plane wing and it succeeded in predicting the tipping point, suggesting it can potentially help with future aeronautical and aerospace designs.

@Caltech news: https://t.co/5I6toiY5FJ

@PNASNews paper: https://t.co/4UsaFwogjT

items.title: Document extraction is an arbitrarily complex reasoning problem for both frontier models and humans....
items.content:
Document extraction is an arbitrarily complex reasoning problem for both frontier models and humans.

✅ The schema encodes essentially hundreds of interrelated reasoning tasks
✅ A PDF can be hundreds or even thousands of pages - it’s an open-world information environment for LLMs to explore (similar to why gdp.pdf is hard)
✅ Solving even a single task is a hard reasoning problem over this environment, where the right dependencies must be reasoned over
✅ The information can be scattered across extraordinarily complex dimensions, from sections, tables, charts, diagrams, handwriting, and more.

Document work is a microcosm of knowledge work as a whole. We’re invested in developing the hardest benchmarks that reflect real-world professional work, challenge the capabilities of frontier models, and incentivize specialized model development for document work.

NVIDIA's FlashInfer and vLLM optimizations incl...
items.content:
The hardware work reaches across the serving stack.

NVIDIA's FlashInfer and vLLM optimizations include fused norm/gating/residual kernels, TEP pooler/unpooler sharding with fused MNNVL collectives, and an FP32-norm-to-TF32-router path.

AMD MI355X supports FP8 and MXFP4 with TP/PP on ROCm.

Initial TPU support uses TorchTPU. With DSpark (acceptance length = 6), Muse Spark Open megakernels reach over 650 tokens/sec on 4 TPU v7 chips and 960 tokens/sec on 8 chips; without speculation, over 270 and 350 tokens/sec. Code access is available through the team or Google.

4/6

items.content:
Inside Muse Spark Open: latent MoE and hybrid attention.

Learned pooler and unpooler projections take the 8,192-wide hidden state down to 4,096 for expert computation, then restore it. All 62 decoder layers use MoE, with 256 experts per layer.

46 layers use a 2,048-token sliding window; 16 attend to the full context. Image and video inputs use a Perception Encoder, with a separate 118M audio encoder.

2/6

items.title: The article addresses a growing problem in the age of LLMs: machine-generated text can closely mimic...
items.content:
The article addresses a growing problem in the age of LLMs: machine-generated text can closely mimic human writing, which makes it harder to verify who or what produced a given piece of content and raises risks of misinformation, impersonation, and unauthorized reuse. A common defense is text watermarking, which hides a detectable signature in generated text. However, most existing methods embed the signature at the level of individual words or word-level statistics, and these signals tend to break down as soon as the text is paraphrased or lightly edited. The article argues this fragility is a serious practical weakness, since paraphrasing is easy and widely available, and it proposes a different place to hide the watermark: not in the words, but in the underlying meaning of each sentence.

The article's main objective is to introduce and evaluate SWAN, a framework that embeds watermark signatures into the semantic structure of sentences using Abstract Meaning Representation (AMR), a graph-based way of representing the core meaning of a sentence independently of its exact wording. The central claim the article tests is that if a signature lives in the meaning structure rather than the surface text, then any paraphrase that preserves meaning should automatically preserve the watermark. The article evaluates whether this approach can match existing methods on ordinary watermarked text while being substantially more robust when that text is rewritten.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/9b8pGzIeIn

items.title: .@davidshor explains why voters are skeptical of UBI, but respond strongly to promises of guaranteed...
items.content:
.@davidshor explains why voters are skeptical of UBI, but respond strongly to promises of guaranteed jobs and income if AI replaces them:

"70% of voters believe that the government has an economic responsibility to help people who have lost their jobs because of AI."

"Normally, ‘We should tax corporations to help disadvantaged people’ is usually very 50/50. In the context of AI, a lot of the libertarianism of voters disappears. Even Trump voters support intervention by a 61 to 20 margin. This is the least polarized I’ve ever seen any question that involved taxing and redistribution."

"The Bernie Sanders policy, ‘We should take a 50% stake in the labs,’ is really quite unpopular. But ‘What if we took the profits from these AI companies and sent them as checks?’ That’s more popular."

"We’ve tested tons of videos on AI economic policy, and the crazier videos do better. People in DC really don’t wanna seem weird. It’s a very conformist place. Whoever speaks with a sci-fi register first, whether they’re Democrats or Republicans, are gonna end up paying really high dividends."

"The very top testing thing: ‘If AI takes your job, you got a new one. Your income is protected. Your healthcare is protected. Your housing is protected. And we’re gonna pay for it by making the billionaires who profit from AI pay their fair share.’ I don’t know if that’s possible."

"In a literal sense, it probably isn’t. But that is probably the direction the political system is gonna go in."

items.summary: MTS Live quotes pollster David Shor on AI economic policy: 70% of voters believe government should help workers displaced by AI, with unusually low polarization (even Trump voters favor intervention 61-20); direct profit-funded checks poll better than government stakes in AI labs, and sci-fi-toned messaging videos test well.
items.reasoning: Data-driven political analysis of AI-displacement attitudes from a top pollster; unique polling insight with modest but targeted engagement, relevant to AI policy discourse.

items.title: LLMs are powerful but expensive to run: every parameter is typically used for every input token, dri...
items.content:
LLMs are powerful but expensive to run: every parameter is typically used for every input token, driving up latency, compute cost, and energy use. Sparse "mixture-of-experts" (MoE) architectures avoid this by activating only a small subset of parameters per token, but training such models from scratch is costly and unstable. An appealing alternative is to convert an existing dense model into a sparse MoE — a process known as MoEfication — yet current conversion methods rely on heuristic rules (random splits, weight-similarity, or activation-pattern clustering) that assign neurons to experts without regard for how those neurons actually affect the model's output.

The article introduces DOT-MoE, a framework that reformulates this neuron-assignment problem as an optimal transport problem: neurons are "shipped" to experts under strict capacity constraints (each expert gets exactly the same number of neurons), with the assignment optimized directly against the network's final output rather than intermediate proxies. Using differentiable optimization and a technique that allows gradients to pass through discrete decisions, DOT-MoE jointly learns which neurons belong to which expert and how tokens should be routed among experts, so the two can adapt to each other. The dense model's weights remain frozen; only the assignment and routing parameters are trained, in a short alignment phase (a few hours on eight GPUs for an 8B-parameter model), followed optionally by light fine-tuning on roughly 1.2 billion tokens.

items.title: Ex-OpenAI researcher Nick Cammarata says the biggest AI models aren’t the black boxes the field once...
items.content:
Ex-OpenAI researcher Nick Cammarata says the biggest AI models aren’t the black boxes the field once feared.

His 2023 OAI project could explain about 1.7% of a model’s neurons. Now at AI research startup Goodfire, he says most are understandable in models up to trillions of parameters.

“I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon.”

items.title: Reliable detection of AI-written text is increasingly important for protecting trust in settings suc...
items.content:
Reliable detection of AI-written text is increasingly important for protecting trust in settings such as research, online communications, and fraud prevention. Yet detectors that rely on statistical or stylistic shortcuts can falter as language models change, and they often struggle to distinguish fully AI-generated writing from human work that has merely been edited by AI. The article addresses this gap by creating a broader evaluation dataset and testing a detector designed to explain its judgments rather than classify text as an opaque black box.

The article introduces AIGC-textbank, a dataset of about 1.5 million examples across 10 domains and 12 language models. It includes pre-ChatGPT human writing, text generated from summaries of human examples, and human writing polished by AI. It also presents REVEAL, an 8-billion-parameter model trained first to produce reasoned explanations and then refined through reinforcement learning, with emphasis on uncertain cases and consistency between evidence and verdict. The researchers evaluated it on five benchmarks, including tests of domain transfer, adversarial perturbations, and mixed human–AI authorship.

For example, you can have a travel assistant agent respond with a hotel card, a map, and an interactive UI that compares plane tickets instead of a wall of text.

• You decide which components you want to use
• The model decides how to combine them for each request
• OpenUI renders the interface

items.title: Open-ended team decisions often involve competing priorities rather than one objectively correct ans...
items.content:
Open-ended team decisions often involve competing priorities rather than one objectively correct answer. Simple artificial-intelligence summaries can make a group’s views easier to digest, but may flatten disagreement, lose minority perspectives, or omit the reasons behind a recommendation. The article evaluates whether a system that represents individual preferences and lets those viewpoints interact can produce more useful, inclusive team outcomes.

The article introduces TeamFusion, which creates a preference-based proxy for each participant, runs a structured discussion among the proxies, and turns that discussion into a draft summary or design. Teams can then critique the result and repeat the process. The authors tested the approach on two tasks: synthesizing public comments and revising advertising designs. The civic task used 500 simulated teams drawn from comments on ten questions. The design evaluation used 50 advertising scenarios, preferences from nine professional designers, and 100 simulated team settings. TeamFusion was compared with direct summarization and other methods that add reasoning, revision, or generic agent discussion.

Read with an AI tutor: https://t.co/XI6gRnc2Wk

The article studies a sequential decision problem in which an agent repeatedly chooses among actions but must pay a cost to observe the reward from the chosen action. The cost can differ by action. This matters in real settings such as online advertising, where testing premium audiences is expensive, and generative AI evaluation, where expert feedback on complex outputs can be costly. In these settings, the usual exploration-exploitation tradeoff becomes a three-way tradeoff among exploring, earning rewards, and deciding whether information is worth its price.

The article's main objective is to characterize and minimize regret when reward observations are optional, action-dependent in cost, and potentially correlated across similar actions. It asks how to design algorithms that decide not only which actions to play but also when to pay for feedback, and what measures capture the difficulty of that problem.

items.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is the first model in NVIDIA's new Bolt family. It scores 21.4 on the...
items.content:
Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is the first model in NVIDIA's new Bolt family. It scores 21.4 on the Intelligence Index, placing 4th among models under 100B parameters and first among US models in that class

Bolt scores 8.6 points above Nemotron 3 Super (12.8) with 39% fewer total parameters. Against Nemotron 3 Ultra, it leads on AutomationBench-AA (15.5% vs 3.0%) and AA-Briefcase (912 vs 874 Elo), but trails on AA-LCR (70% vs 79%) and Humanity's Last Exam (25% vs 28%)

Things are getting crazy: This platform lets you build an app and use it to do your work.

It's both the Builder and the Operator.

1. You want to build an invoicing app, so you describe it to Proto and specify the fields you want to track.

2. Proto turns your description into the invoicing app. It creates the data structures, views, and workflows you need.

3. You verify the invoicing app and make sure everything works.

4. From here, you can tell Proto to start invoicing your clients by using the app it just built.

items.content:
Outlier Detection in Python — https://t.co/l5qPXcl0ul
——
#Statistics #DataScientist #DataScience
——
I have always appreciated the unusual, unexpected, and surprising in science and in data. As famous science author Arthur C. Clarke once said, “The most exciting phrase to hear in science, the one that heralds new discoveries, is not ‘Eureka!’ (I found it) but ‘That’s funny!’” This is the primary reason that I motivated most of the doctoral students that I mentored at GMU to work on some variation of Novelty Discovery (or Surprise Discovery) for their Ph.D. dissertations.

“Surprise discovery” for me is a much more positive, exciting phrase than “outlier detection” or “anomaly detection”, and it is much richer in meaning, in algorithms, and in new opportunities. Finding the surprising unexpected thing in your data is what inspires our exclamation “That’s funny!”, which may be signaling a great discovery (either about your data’s quality, or about your data pipeline’s deficiencies, or about some wholly new scientific concept = SURPRISE DISCOVERY!). As famous astronomer Vera Rubin said, “Science progresses best when new observations (data) force us to alter our preconceptions.”

items.title: Measured on a pre-release @DeepInfra endpoint serving NVFP4 weights, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL reaches a...
items.content:
Measured on a pre-release @DeepInfra endpoint serving NVFP4 weights, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL reaches an output speed of ~630 tokens/s with 100k-token prompts. That is the fastest of any model scoring 20 or more on the Intelligence Index that we have measured at this prompt length

That is ~5x Inkling Small (124 tokens/s), ~2.7x Nemotron 3 Ultra (235), and ~4.5x Nemotron 3 Super (140). It also returns its first token in 1.8s, against 4.4s for Nemotron 3 Ultra and 8.5s for Inkling Small

@proto...
items.content:
Most companies still spend months setting up business software before anyone gets to use it.

@protosphinx and the https://t.co/7eSjDZzkLP team are betting that turns into a conversation. You describe a process you know, like chasing overdue invoices, and their agent Proto builds the app. Then it does the work inside that app, and sensitive steps can wait for a person to sign off.

People using it by hand pay $0 per seat. You only pay when the agent does the work.

If agents end up doing more of the work, does it still make sense to pay for software by the seat?

Pick one business process you know. 

Try building it with https://t.co/7eSjDZzkLP and Proto, then judge the result yourself. https://

https://t.co/AioMLNiuM6

items.content:
Prices for these systems are approximate and shift from week to week. At current prices the $5,900 RTX Spark laptop costs more than the MacBook Pro (~$3,700) and Ryzen AI Halo ($4,000) but slightly less than DGX Spark (~$6,000), and the GeForce RTX 5090 desktop (~$9,500 with a ~$7,000 card) is the most expensive

At these prices, the more a system costs, the faster it completes our workload on every model we test. We expect that to change as we add more systems and runtimes. Our leaderboard lets you enter your own prices

—
...
items.content:
Linear Algebra and Optimization for Machine Learning [516-page textbook]: https://t.co/s6oCEvVMKS
—
This textbook is organized around its 2 main themes: [Amazon Summary]

1. Linear algebra and its applications: The chapters focus on the basics of linear algebra together with their common applications to singular value decomposition, matrix factorization, similarity matrices (kernel methods), and graph analysis. Numerous machine learning applications have been used as examples, such as spectral clustering, kernel-based classification, and outlier detection. The tight integration of linear algebra methods with examples from machine learning differentiates this book from generic volumes on linear algebra. The focus is clearly on the most relevant aspects of linear algebra for machine learning and to teach readers how to apply these concepts.

2. Optimization and its applications: Much of machine learning is posed as an optimization problem in which we try to maximize the accuracy of regression and classification models. The “parent problem” of optimization-centric machine learning is least-squares regression. Interestingly, this problem arises in both linear algebra and optimization, and is one of the key connecting problems of the two fields. Least-squares regression is also the starting point for support vector machines, logistic regression, and recommender systems. Furthermore, the methods for dimensionality reduction and matrix factorization also require the development of optimization methods. A general view of optimization in computational graphs is discussed together with its applications to back propagation in neural networks.

items.content:
There are two types of companies: sedentary and nomadic.

Sedentary companies settle somewhere and build. Nomadic companies are willing to leave one place and go somewhere new. Sedentary companies build up fixed wealth, like fields and granaries. Nomadic companies build up portable wealth, like their skills and herds. When the climate changes, you see who’s willing to move and what they can take with them.

My Review (on Amazon):
I love this book, not only for its amazing content, but also for its brilliant adherence to its "Cookbook" label. The table of contents looks repetitive, but that's the magic of it. Find the algorithm, method, or application that you want "to cook up," and the presentation follows a uniform format from chapter to chapter. This is an extraordinarily practical, useful, and reader-friendly style, perfect for the target audience: anyone who needs to use (or is discovering how to use) specific Scikit-learn tools for their Python-based machine learning tasks. Consequently, this is great not only for individual use but also for training workshops and other educational settings. Python code in a cookbook context has never looked so good. IMHO.

Amazon Summary:
“Google Cloud Platform offers significant scalability, but managing costs effectively is critical to realizing its value. The Cloud FinOps Playbook for Google Cloud is a practical guide to managing cloud spend and driving financial accountability on GCP.

This book covers the dual role of AI in FinOps, that is, using AI for FinOps through agentic cost management, and applying FinOps for AI by establishing cost governance over AI workloads. You'll build automation for reporting and forecasting, implement quota guardrails, and drive financial accountability across engineering, finance, and operations teams.”

items.title: The Scientific Computing course notes by Jeffrey R. Chasnov (2013) is now in @ChapterPal's collectio...
items.content:
The Scientific Computing course notes by Jeffrey R. Chasnov (2013) is now in @ChapterPal's collection of open textbooks.

This volume is a set of lecture-based textbook notes for readers with a mathematical background, especially mathematics majors, who want to learn how computation can solve problems that resist direct analytic treatment. It assumes no previous study of numerical analysis. 

Calculus supports much of the numerical material, and multivariable calculus is useful for the fluid mechanics chapters; the book also introduces MATLAB as a working tool.

The book connects core numerical algorithms with two extended areas of application: nonlinear dynamical systems and computational fluid dynamics.

It begins with the limits of computer number representation and the effects of round-off, then develops methods for finding roots, integrating functions, solving ordinary differential equations, and handling linear systems.

Further chapters cover finite-difference approximations, iterative solvers, interpolation, and least-squares fitting. Across these topics, the organizing concerns are accuracy, error, convergence, computational cost, and the practical choice of method. The presentation explains how algorithms are built and used, while explicitly giving limited attention to the deeper theory of numerical analysis.

Read the textbook with an AI tutor: https://t.co/EMVC8mgutF

All books on ChapterPal are free to read with a free account. A paid account gives you more questions to ask the AI tutor, personalized reading recommendations based on your interests, auto-generated quizzes that allow you to validate your understanding, offline reading with a mobile app, and more.

Table of contents:

Front Matter
  Preface
Part I: Numerical Methods
  Chapter 1: IEEE Arithmetic
    - Definitions
    - IEEE double precision format
  Chapter 2: Root Finding
    - Bisection Method
    - Newton’s Method
      * Estimate 2 using x0=1
    - Secant Method
      * Newton’s Method
      * Secant Method
  Chapter 3: Integration
      * Simpson’s rule
  Chapter 4: Differential Equations
    - Initial value problem
      * Euler method
      * Higher-order Runge-Kutta methods
      * Adaptive Runge-Kutta Methods
  Chapter 5: Linear Algebra
    - LU decomposition
    - MATLAB programming
  Chapter 6: Finite Difference Approximation
    - Finite difference formulas
  Chapter 7: Iterative Methods
    - Newton’s method for a system of nonlinear equations
  Chapter 8: Interpolation
    - Piecewise linear interpolation
    - Cubic spline interpolation
  Chapter 9: Least-Squares Approximation
Part II: Dynamical Systems and Chaos
  Chapter 10: The Simple Pendulum
    - Governing equations
      * Analytical solution
  Chapter 11: The Damped, Driven Pendulum
    - The nonlinear pendulum
  Chapter 12: Concepts and Tools
    - Fixed points and linear stability analysis
    - Saddle-node bifurcation
    - Pitchfork bifurcations
      * Supercritical pitchfork bifurcation
    - Limit cycles
    - Attractors and basins of attraction
    - Poincaré sections
    - Fractal dimensions
    - Classical fractals
      * Cantor set
      * Koch curve
      * Numerical computation
  Chapter 13: Pendulum Dynamics
    - Spontaneous symmetry-breaking bifurcation
    - Period doubling in the logistic map
    - Computation of the Feigenbaum constant
Part III: Computational Fluid Dynamics
  Chapter 14: The Governing Equations
    - Multi-variable calculus
      * Vector algebra
    - Momentum equation
      * Material derivative
  Chapter 15: Laminar Flow
    - Plane Couette flow
    - Pipe flow
  Chapter 16: Stream Function, Vorticity Equations
    - Stream function
  Chapter 17: Flow Past an Obstacle
    - Flow past a rectangle
    - Finite difference approximation
    - Boundary conditions
    - Solution using Newton’s method

items.title: To make it a bit more clearer what Hotelist does to show you the real ratings of hotels, instead of ...
items.content:
To make it a bit more clearer what Hotelist does to show you the real ratings of hotels, instead of the inflated ratings from booking sites

I've added this toggle for @afonsolfm as he didn't understand what was the point

On booking sites this hotel below would look good or great based on the ratings (except maybe Yelp), like an 8.8/10 must be great?

When we take the average range of ratings on each booking site though, for example 4.2 to 5 and then take its hotel rating of 4.5, we can then discover the real rating of the hotel by normalizing it inside that range

Then we end up with a rating of 1.88/5, very different right?

So that's how you can find real ratings of hotels on Hotelist! 🙏

When we take the average range of ratings on each booking site though, for example 4.2 to 5 and then take its hotel rating of 4.5, we can then discover the real rating of the hotel by normalizing it inside that range

Then we end up with a rating of 1.88/5, very different right?

So that's how you can find real ratings of hotels on Hotelist! 🙏

items.title: Fixed Point-Theorem! In 1900, Dutch mathematician L. E. J. Brouwer established a remarkable Result: ...
items.content:
Fixed Point-Theorem! In 1900, Dutch mathematician L. E. J. Brouwer established a remarkable Result: Every continuous function mapping a closed disk into itself must leave at least a point unchanged.

The remarkable part? Mathematics guarantees that such a point exists without telling us where it is located!

A foundational result in topology with applications in game theory, economics, and mathematical analysis. Some numbers may be rounded off.
